fixes.explanation: Yes, friend. "When the righteous flourish, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan." The proverb sets two situations side by side, and each one has its own sound. Rejoicing goes with the righteous flourishing, and groaning goes with the wicked ruling.
Guards isn't what the verse says, friend. The companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth. The man who loves wisdom shows up in the first half, where the verse says he brings joy to his father.

Doubling would be quite a deal, friend, and I'd have questions about the oven that did it. But the verse says this man squanders his wealth. Doubling goes the opposite direction. The proverb has no good news about the money in this one.
A seed in a field is a nice picture, friend, but this proverb isn't about farming. Nothing in the verse mentions a field. It says the flatterer spreads a net for his feet, and a net is for catching.

I get the second-guessing, friend, but the proverb says exactly that. "An evil man is caught by his own sin…" His own sin is what catches him. Then the verse flips to the righteous one, who sings and rejoices. I'd rather be the one singing.

Yes, friend. The righteous consider the cause of the poor, but the wicked have no regard for such concerns. One side considers the cause of the poor, and the other has no regard for it. That's the contrast in one verse.

That would at least be something, but it isn't what the proverb says. The wicked have no regard for such concerns. Giving a little and moving on isn't in the verse. The ones who consider the cause of the poor are the righteous.
Rumors do spread fast, friend, but that isn't the word here. The wise turn away anger. The mockers are the ones who inflame a city. Anger is the thing the wise turn away.

I'd love that for him, but the verse doesn't say it. It says there will be raving and laughing with no resolution. A fast ruling for the wise man isn't in the verse. The word it uses is no resolution.
Right, it's false, friend. The proverb says if a ruler listens to lies, all his officials will be wicked. That's all of them, not just a few. A few and all are very different numbers.

Yes, friend, and it's a big one. "The poor man and the oppressor have this in common: The LORD gives light to the eyes of both." Those two couldn't be further apart, and yet this one thing is the same for both. The verse says it plainly and I'll leave it there.

Yes, friend, that's the word. "A rod of correction imparts wisdom, but a child left to himself disgraces his mother." The verse is talking about the child left to himself. Disgraces is a heavy word, so I'll leave it at what the verse says.

Joy goes with the people rejoicing back in verse 2, when the righteous flourish. Here, when the wicked thrive, the verse says rebellion increases. Joy isn't what it says increases. Different people thriving, different results.

Yes, friend, those are the two. "Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will bring delight to your soul." Rest and delight are the things the verse names. Anybody who's ever wanted a quiet evening knows how good that sounds.

That's the one, friend. "…but blessed is he who keeps the Law." The verse swings on that little word but. First come the people casting off restraint where there is no vision, then comes the blessing for the one who keeps the Law.
Forgetting isn't what the proverb says. It says he understands but will not respond. The understanding is already there, and the verse doesn't mention his memory. What's missing is the response.

Yes, friend. "A servant pampered from his youth will bring grief in the end." Notice the words in the end. It starts in his youth and lands at the end, kind of like a batch that only tells you how it went when it comes out of the oven.
I'd love some praise, but that's not what this verse hands out. The pampered servant will bring grief in the end. Grief is what he brings, friend, not applause.

That's right, friend. "A man’s pride will bring him low, but a humble spirit will obtain honor." Pride is headed up in its own mind, but the verse says it brings him low. The humble spirit is the one that obtains honor. I think the honor side of that deal looks better.

Yes, it's true, friend. "…a humble spirit will obtain honor." The verse sets two roads side by side: pride, which brings a man low, and a humble spirit, which obtains honor. I think honor is the better deal.

Yes, friend. "Many seek the ruler’s favor, but a man receives justice from the LORD." The verse says many seek the ruler's favor, and then it turns. Seeking a ruler's favor and receiving justice are two different things here, and justice comes from the LORD.

That's right, friend. "An unjust man is detestable to the righteous, and one whose way is upright is detestable to the wicked." Each side finds the other detestable. It's the last verse of the chapter, and it ends right there.
A friend is the opposite of what the verse says. One whose way is upright is detestable to the wicked. Detestable is the word to hold onto here.
The proverb doesn't call him a mystery, friend. It says the upright man is detestable to the wicked. Detestable is the word the verse uses for how they see him.
